cues.text: Disciple of the Apostles
Polycarp was born about the year 69 and became Bishop of Smyrna in Asia Minor.
He belonged to the last generation to have known the Apostles in person.
He had been instructed by them and, in particular, was a disciple of St. John , from whom he received the faith he would guard and hand on through a long life.
St. Ignatius of Antioch , passing through Smyrna on his way to martyrdom, embraced him as a friend and later wrote him a letter of encouragement.
A Link in the Chain
Polycarp's chief historical importance is as a bridge between the age of the Apostles and the age of the Fathers.
His own disciple St. Irenaeus of Lyons never forgot him.
He recorded how the old bishop would speak of his conversations with John and with others who had seen the Lord, and how his teaching agreed in everything with the Scriptures.
Through this living chain the Church could trace her doctrine, unbroken, from Christ to the Apostles to men still alive in the second century.
The Roman Visit

Late in life Polycarp travelled to Rome to confer with Pope Anicetus, chiefly over the date on which Easter should be kept, a question on which the churches of Asia and of Rome followed different customs.

The two could not persuade one another, yet they parted in peace and communion, Anicetus inviting Polycarp to celebrate the Eucharist in his own church — an early and gracious model of unity amid disagreement.
While in Rome Polycarp encountered Marcion, whom he rejected as a heretic.
Letter to the Philippians
One work of Polycarp survives, his Letter to the Philippians , written in answer to a request from that church and forwarding to them the letters of Ignatius.

Modest and pastoral, steeped in the language of the New Testament, it exhorts the faithful to righteousness, patience, and steadfastness, and confirms from an eyewitness the early use of the apostolic writings.
It is a plain, humble document from a man who cared more for fidelity than for eloquence.
The Age of the Martyrs
The account of Polycarp's death, sent by the church of Smyrna to another congregation, is more than the record of one man's courage.
It is the earliest surviving document to reflect on martyrdom itself.
It distinguishes true witness from reckless self-offering.
It also describes how the faithful gathered up the martyr's bones, more precious than costly stones, to keep his memory and to celebrate each year the day of his birth into heaven.
In this the little letter stands at the head of a long tradition.
That tradition is the Christian veneration of the martyrs, the keeping of their relics, and the honouring of their heavenly birthdays, which shapes the calendar of the Church to this day.
Arrest and Trial
When persecution broke out at Smyrna and the crowd bayed for the bishop, Polycarp withdrew to a farm, but was betrayed and arrested.
Brought before the proconsul in the stadium, he was urged to save his life by swearing by Caesar and reviling Christ.
His answer has echoed through the centuries: eighty-six years he had served his King, who had never wronged him — how then could he blaspheme the one who saved him?
Threatened with fire, he replied that the proconsul's fire burned for an hour and then was quenched, but he did not fear it.
Martyrdom by Fire
Polycarp was bound to the stake and the pyre lit, about the year 155.
The eyewitness account, the Martyrdom of Polycarp sent out by his own church, relates that the flames arched around him like a sail without consuming him, so that at last he was killed with a dagger.
It is the earliest detailed record of a Christian martyrdom outside the New Testament, and the source of much later devotion to the relics of the martyrs.
His feast is kept on February 23 , and with Ignatius and Clement he stands among the Apostolic Fathers.
